title: Ministry introduced Anganwadi cum Creches under Palna for providing day care creche facilities in safe and secure environment to children
body_text:
The Ministry introduced Anganwadi cum Creches (AWCCs) under Palna Scheme w.e.f. 01 April 2022, for providing day care creche facilities in safe and secure environment to children (aged 06 months – 06 years) of all mothers irrespective of their employment status along with nutritional support, health and cognitive development of children, growth monitoring, immunization, education etc. Palna component under Samarthya vertical of Mission Shakti is a centrally sponsored scheme and is implemented with a funding ratio of 60:40 between Centre and State Governments and UTs with legislature except North East & Special Category States where ratio is 90:10. For UTs without legislature, 100% funding is provided by the Central Government. Funds under the Scheme are released to the States/UTs in accordance with the guidelines of the Department of Expenditure through the Single Nodal Agency (SNA)/SNA-SPARSH mechanism of the Public Financial Management System (PFMS). Presently, a total of 4,172 Anganwadi-cum-Crèches (AWCCs) are operational across the country.
Ministry of Labour and Employment has informed that the provisions of the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 have been subsumed under the Code on Social Security, 2020, which came into effect on 21.11.2025. Section 67 of the Code on Social Security, 2020 provides for creche facilities for establishment with 50 or more employees. Under the Code, enforcement in respect of establishments under the State Sphere is the responsibility of the respective State Governments. Chief Labour Commissioner (Central) Organisation under the Ministry of Labour and Employment is the designated enforcement authority for ensuring compliance with maternity benefit provisions in establishments under the Central Sphere.
This information was given by the Minister of State for Women and Child Development Smt. Savitri Thakur in Rajya Sabha in reply to a question.

ministry.name: Ministry of Women and Child Development

enrichment.summary: The Ministry of Women and Child Development informed the Rajya Sabha that Anganwadi-cum-Crèches (AWCCs) under the Palna Scheme, launched from 1 April 2022, currently number 4,172 operational units across India, providing day-care facilities for children aged 6 months to 6 years regardless of their mothers' employment status. Palna is a centrally sponsored scheme under the Samarthya vertical of Mission Shakti, funded on a 60:40 Centre-State basis (90:10 for NE/special category states, 100% for UTs without legislature). The reply also noted that the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961 has been subsumed under the Code on Social Security, 2020 (effective 21.11.2025), whose Section 67 mandates creche facilities for establishments with 50 or more employees.
enrichment.context:
The Palna scheme reflects the government's shift toward integrating child-care infrastructure with women's workforce participation, recognizing that lack of safe crèche facilities is a major barrier to female labour force participation in India. It builds on the Anganwadi network established under the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme, repurposing existing Anganwadi infrastructure to also serve as day-care centres, thus optimizing resources rather than creating entirely new institutions. Mission Shakti, under which Palna's Samarthya vertical falls, is an umbrella scheme for women's safety, security, and empowerment, consolidating earlier schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao, One Stop Centres, and Ujjawala.

The mention of the Code on Social Security, 2020 is significant as it represents one of the four labour codes that consolidate 29 central labour laws, aimed at simplifying compliance while extending certain protections. Section 67's creche mandate for establishments with 50+ employees continues a provision that existed under the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017, but now operates within the broader labour codification framework. The dual governance structure—Central Sphere enforcement via the Chief Labour Commissioner and State Sphere enforcement by state governments—highlights ongoing federalism challenges in labour law implementation in India.
